newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa trade wary as long holder sticks to his guns.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa trade wary as long holder sticks to his guns.

text.p: Six months ago traders had written off the influential cocoa trader who is said to hold at least a quarter of world stocks.
But he is again calling the shots, threatening to send futures prices spiralling up.

A surge in prices this month has focused traders' minds on trying to second guess what Anthony Ward, director of U.S. trade house Phibro, may have in mind for some 300,000 tonnes of cocoa he was believed by traders to have stockpiled from the London exchange in September.

Ward's position was the driving force behind a rise to eight-year peaks of 1,172 stg a tonne in June, but prices then collapsed amid a slew of West African shipments to European ports, and the Phibro factor was largely brushed aside. But things are changing again.
"The game is not over. We are probably in the first set," said one London trader.
"People had been rather complacent about the whole thing. They thought 'prices are so low, he's dead and buried'. Now they are taking his position more seriously."

The tide turned last month when Phibro rolled its shorts in March futures forward to December even as prices were stuck in a vicious downtrend, implying that it has no intention of delivering the cocoa back, at least for the time being.
Last week Ward injected a further chill to an already jumpy market, saying he expected prices to hit 1,500 sterling per tonne by the summer from just over 1,000 sterling at present.

"I think the value of cocoa is very low and I expect the price to reach 1,500 pounds by the summer and many thousand pounds within three to six years," he said on the fringes of a cocoa meeting in London.
His optimism wasn't surprising since one trader calculated that a 500-stg rise in the price of cocoa would net Phibro some 200 million stg on 400,000 tonnes of cocoa.
But what sent shivers across the market was Ward's clear signal that his strategy is to hold out for long term gains. "The idea is to make money," he said.
The market will move in his favour if global consumption rises and supply deficits widen, as many analysts predict. But this may take years.
"We've got supply and demand and we've got Phibro. If Phibro decides they want to squeeze the market they can push it up to an extraordinary degree," said one commodity markets analyst.

Identifying Phibro's physical stocks amid a constant juggling of futures, options and currencies in London and New York is not an easy business. But traders reckon they must be somewhere between 300,000 and 500,000 tonnes.

How long Phibro can afford to keep such a hefty position depends on the depth of its coffers. Warehouse and insurance costs can run into millions of sterling and the stock is still showing a loss, at least as far as current prices are concerned.
But the trade house is believed to be financing the physical carry by forward short positions, possibly in December and distant March and May, traders said.
Phibro's fortunes hang on a downturn in Ivory Coast's production -- the world's biggest -- after a torrent of crop arrivals in the last two years, and a resulting tightness in supplies.

Benchmark cocoa prices surged to a seven-month high of 1,048 stg a tonne last week from a low of 855 stg just a month ago. But the move was inspired by chart signals, while the fundamental picture remains gloomy.
But analysts believe rising chocolate consumption, especially in the Far East, will outpace production growth in the coming years.
They say that even assuming standard consumption growth of around 3-3.5 percent a year the market would be looking at a big deficit in the coming 1997/98 season.
And if there was a large deficit this year, Phibro would have an opportunity to squeeze the market, particularly if it picked up some more cocoa.
But huge Ivorian crops in the last two years forced analysts to tone down previous such tight supply scenarios and there is nothing concrete to suggest a trend change.

For the 1996/97 season crop experts initially forecast an Ivorian harvest of around 800,000 tonnes. But the crop is now looking more like 1.1 million tonnes, just short of last year's record of 1.2 million.
The end-year deficit was first projected at some 300,000 tonnes. Now most estimates have come down to around 100,000.

"It's always the case that every year the following year is going to be a big deficit year...half way through the year you have revise it down. But if you stick to your guns long enough you will be right one time," said one analyst.
While Phibro sticks to its guns, industry buyers see no rush to cover against a future squeeze.
"We have been here last year and the game is still on," said a cocoa buyer for a large UK based chocolate manufacturer.
